fullText:
Wisconsin's inability to stay out of the penalty box proved costly in a battle against its top rival.

In a matchup of the nation's top-ranked women's hockey teams, the top-ranked Badgers allowed two power-play goals in the third period and lost 2-1 to Ohio State at OSU Ice Rink in Columbus, Ohio.

The game was the WCHA opener for the Badgers and the first of four regular-season matchups between teams that have played in the last four NCAA finals.

The heroes for the Buckeyes (5-0, 3-0 WCHA) were junior defender Mira Jungaker and sophomore forwards Hilda Svensson. The pair had a hand in each of the team's goals.

Svensson scored the game-winner at the 16:20 mark of the third period off passes from Jungaker and sophomore forward Sanni Vanhanen.

Here are three takeaways from the game

When UW (4-1, 0-1) looks back at this game, it will look at the final period when it was outshot, 19-3.

Senior goaltender Ava McNaughton tied a career-high with 38 saves. She made five saves to keep the Buckeyes scoreless during their first three power plays.

On Ohio State's fourth power play, Jungaker got a shot through traffic and past McNaughton to tie the game at the 7:01 mark of the period.

Both teams were playing a skater short when Adela Sapovalivova was called for roughing on senior Kaia Malachino in front of the crease just after a McNaughton save. Fifty-two seconds later Svensson scored the game-winner.

It's only October, but the intensity between the two rivals was in mid-season form.

Wisconsin received three roughing penalties and elbow and was penalized nine times. The teams combined for 17 penalties which cost 34 minutes of ice time.

Hall gives the Badgers the lead 😮‍💨

A: Potter, Scannell pic.twitter.com/TZyISoOz9Q

Considering the number of penalties, it was fitting that UW scored on a power play as well.

Senior Cassie Hall scored off passes from junior Laney Potter and Maggie Scannell at the 14:43 mark.

The Badgers were 29-34 on faceoffs, but Sapovalivova won a faceoff in the Badgers zone. Scannell controled the puck and passed it back to Potter, who fired it to Hall across the ice to the top fo the circle.

The play was the highlight of a second period when Wisconsin played its, going even with the Buckeyes in shots on goal (10-10) and creating three power play chances.

title: Boxing Mailbag: Roy Jones Jr as a heavyweight, trainer importance, more
description: Who’s the best heavyweight champ Roy Jones Jr could have beaten? Plus more!
fullText:
How much difference do you think a trainer can make? If you were building a fighter from the ground up, what trainer would you choose to develop him? If you had to pick a trainer to get a world level fighter ready for one big fight, who would you choose?

I think a trainer CAN make a lot of difference. I've said before that I think trainers get too much credit when fighters are doing well, and too much blame when they aren't. There are obviously exceptions to that idea, and those exceptions are always pretty clear. But end of the day the fighter has to execute the game plan, and I think you can generally get a sense when it's a bad plan vs when it's a tough performance.

The biggest thing is the mesh of personalities with trainer and fighter. That doesn't get enough focus, you can take a truly great trainer

And honestly, if I were picking a trainer and everyone ever is available, it'd definitely be one of the old-timers, someone long dead like Eddie Futch, even if they don't understand what a "pool noodle" even is. If I had to pick from today's field, I'd go Robert Garcia.

A short one, open to everyone – who's the boxer who reinvented himself the most in your opinion, past or present. There's often sentiment (right more often than wrong) that trainer hopping, especially past the age of 30 won't help, as in "can't teach old dog new tricks." But have there been cases where that actually did happen?

Let me open this one up to answers from the questions thread, because these would be two possible picks by me, and these comments already said what I would say, basically.

Tyler Neves: "For me, Manny Pacquiao immediately comes to mind. He started as a one handed tornado of a fighter and continued evolving to the point where the right hook was possibly an even better weapon than his straight left. As he aged, he settled into a role as more of a boxer puncher and was still successful with a lot less foot movement than what he used in his prime."

Sunzshock: "I'd also shout out Manny Steward and his rebuild of Wlad Klitschko. Transformed him from a glass cannon that got KOed by Corrie Sanders and Lamon Brewster into a very difficult to beat jab and grab dominant champion. 16-0 under Manny Steward. I'd argue they would have kept the streak going and beat Tyson Fury if Steward hadn't left us too young at age 68."

But I always feel mainly limited to what I've seen happen live, in real time, in my life. Those of you older than me or more expertly-versed in history beyond The Big Stuff might have some other answers.

While Roy Jones becoming a champion at middleweight and heavyweight is an all time great accomplishment, John Ruiz was definitely one of the weakest HW champions in history. So who do you think is the best HW champion that RJJ was good enough to beat, regardless of era?

If we're not counting these "WBA regular" types and whatnot, I think the list gets pretty short. Where it gets tough is you could say he might have had a shot with Joe Frazier, Joe wasn't a big guy by modern heavyweight standards — 5'11", about 200-215 lbs in his best years. But I think he hit too hard, and I don't think Roy would have dented him.

Realistically it's probably one of the old time heavyweight champs, who were actually genuine champs but weren't bigger than Roy, really, and might get touched up by him pretty awful. But he'd have to have his jab going against anybody, it'd have to be sharp.

Maybe on paper it seems like he'd have a shot with Usyk, but I don't think he would have done well with Usyk at all.

Boxing is a sport where the name of the game is to "hit and not get hit." Shakur Stevenson is the embodiment of that, but yet he is called "boring." Do you feel like that's a disrespect to the sport of boxing?? Do you find Shakur Stevenson boring?

I find him boring if his fight is boring, which sometimes it is. Sometimes I like watching him more than other people do. The whole thing isn't new to boxing, guys who fight like Shakur have long had problems getting people to want to pay to see them outside of their home area. I can't say I think it's disrespect to boxing, boxing is a spectator sport people spend their time and money on. Maybe the most paywalled sport in the world at this point. They want to be entertainined. Shakur's style is not one that is going to tickle the fancy of the average fan.

What kind of chance do you give Mbilli to beat Canelo?

It's gonna depend on Canelo and what he has left, but there's much more of a realistic chance for Canelo to lose this fight than at any other fight he's had, like, at or nearer to this level than the fights he actually has lost or GGG.

I know you at one time kept some odd hours because fights were almost always 10-11 PM on Friday and Saturday. With a lot more fights emanating out of Britain/Saudi have you shifted your sleeping/working schedule? PS the Olympic boxing overnight threads were always a good time when it was at 4-5 in the morning.

I've kept odd hours pretty much all my life, still do to a degree, but I've also just gotten older. It's a lot closer to normal nowadays, and the changing geographics of boxing have definitely had something to do with that. I do still enjoy an overnighter from Japan or Australia, though. And I loved those Olympic boxing sessions from London, Tokyo, and Paris. Rio was still fun, LA will be, too, but something about starting a day for two weeks with morning boxing really just feels right.

Favourite boxing films? You recommended Fat City during covid, which I bloody loved, and a while ago I recommended Jawbone, have you seen it?

Haven't seen Jawbone. Along with Fat City, I'm a huge fan of Rocky; the sequels are fun junk but the first movie is a pretty great film, and I like Rocky Balboa for moving the material back toward the original tone. I really liked Cinderella Man. I always watched Gladiator (with Brian Dennehy, Cuban Gooding Jr, and James Marshall) and Diggstown when they'd come on Showtime or The Movie Channel when I was a kid, still enjoy both movies. Raging Bull is a great movie, Girlfight is a great movie which I actually hadn't seen until a couple years ago, but I loved it. I liked Creed! I thought the sequels were not as good.

The Harder They Fall with Bogart is a good movie more than a "good boxing movie," but is about boxing within a film noir, and I love that genre. Also it's sort of boxing-adjacent and you'll have to be able to handle watching a musical, but It's Always Fair Weather is a great film, a lot more cynical and downtrodden than the average musical, wasn't a hit on release but has been greater appreciated over the decades.

With it looking increasingly like the Super Bowl window for the Lions is closed or nearly closed, are you, like me, grateful for the return of the SOLs we grew up with? Or do you lament the loss of opportunity to hear weird phrases like "Detroit Lions, Super Bowl Champions"?

Oh, it's closed. I think that team is losing some of its spirit, too, and even more than just him clearly being an excellent offensive football coach, I think we can say now that Ben Johnson played a real role in that team being as peppy and tough as they were, because he's getting that same sort of thing out of Chicago. To me it seems like Campbell's cracking now in his second season of trying to work with a deeply flawed, .500-ish team and lacking the play calling of Johnson yet again. That attempt at a final drive last weekend was horrendous, and the defense can't stop anyone despite Hutchinson's best efforts.

title: Layne Riggs Wins at Charlotte in Thrilling Truck Series Chase Battle
description: Riggs Makes Late Race Pass for Seventh Victory Layne Riggs delivered a huge performance Friday night at Charlotte Motor Speedway, passing championship rival Kaden Honeycutt late in the race to win the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series Ecosave 200. The victory marked Riggs’ seventh win of the 2026 season and gave him a major boost in…
fullText:
Layne Riggs delivered a huge performance Friday night at Charlotte Motor Speedway, passing championship rival Kaden Honeycutt late in the race to win the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series Ecosave 200. The victory marked Riggs' seventh win of the 2026 season and gave him a major boost in the battle for the series championship.

Driving the No. 34 Ford for Front Row Motorsports, Riggs started 13th but quickly worked his way toward the front. He showed strong speed throughout the race, winning Stage 1 and leading 47 of the 134 laps.

However, the biggest moment came during the closing laps, when Riggs found himself battling Honeycutt for the lead.

Honeycutt appeared to be in position to secure another important victory as the race approached its conclusion. The championship leader had led a race-high 85 laps and won Stage 2, putting himself in control for much of the event.

Riggs refused to back down, steadily closing the gap as the laps wound down. With seven laps remaining, he made his move against Honeycutt entering Turn 4.

The pressure proved too much for Honeycutt, who slid up the track and brushed the outside wall. Riggs took advantage of the mistake, moved into the lead and held on through the final laps to secure the win.

Christian Eckes finished second, 0.596 seconds behind Riggs, while Honeycutt recovered to finish third. Bayley Currey and Chandler Smith rounded out the top five.

The race featured several cautions and a late red flag following a multi-truck accident, adding even more drama to an already intense night.

The victory carries major championship implications for Riggs. Entering Charlotte trailing Honeycutt in the standings, Riggs cut the deficit to just 17 points with four postseason races remaining.

The result also completed a season sweep for Riggs at Charlotte, giving him victories in both Truck Series races held at the track in 2026.

With momentum now on his side, Riggs has positioned himself as a serious threat to win the championship. His ability to recover from a 13th-place starting position and execute a late-race pass demonstrated the speed and determination needed during the postseason.

Riggs and Front Row Motorsports will now turn their attention toward the next round of the Truck Series Chase at Phoenix Raceway.

With the championship battle tightening and only four postseason races remaining, every position matters. Riggs has closed the gap considerably, and another strong performance could put even more pressure on Honeycutt.

Friday night's victory was more than another win for Riggs. It was a statement that he intends to fight for the championship until the very end.

title: Bam Adebayo gets honest about how LaMelo Ball injured him and the long-term impact
description: LaMelo Ball made the headlines when he injured Bam Adebayo, but it seems the latter is looking at the bright side.
fullText:
Bam Adebayo gets honest about how LaMelo Ball injured him and the long-term impact originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Miami Heat failed to advance in the Play-In Tournament back in April 2026 because they lost to the Charlotte Hornets. It could have gone either way, but the Heat would have benefited from having Bam Adebayo around, who sustained an injury in the second quarter of that game.

He missed the rest of the matchup because LaMelo Ball grabbed Adebayo's leg while he was falling to the ground. It was not a pretty sight, and Ball got heavily criticized for it. Now, Adebayo has looked back on it, and it seems like he is taking the high ground in a situation where he did nothing wrong.

Heat fans were rightfully frustrated back then because they knew that Adebayo would have made an impact that could have won them that game. Considering Ball was the player who hit the game-winning shot back then, it was truly a bitter day for Heat fans.

Ball did apologize for tripping Adebayo, but it seems he made an excuse about not knowing where he was because he got hit in the head. Of course, it can be a valid explanation, but that did not sit well with the Heat fans. It did not sit well with the NBA either, as he was assessed a retroactive flagrant-2 foul.

MORE: DeMarcus Cousins fires back at the comparisons between his partnership with Anthony Davis and the Heat's frontcourt

Half a year later, it seems that Adebayo is doing his best to move on from the trip. It was a costly one because the Heat's season ended there with Adebayo nursing a back injury from the trip. However, it did get them to a position where they could trade for Giannis Antetokounmpo, so Adebayo is looking at the bright side.

"I don't carry hate in my heart. If you spend that much time thinking about that, then you're not worried about the present and the future. It happened, and it's over with. It's one of those things where you forgive, and you don't forget, but no hate in the heart," Adebayo said about the injury he sustained because of Ball.

"Honestly, it kind of worked out better for us that we lost the game. So, I mean, the positive is it was part of us getting new guys on the team. We got a great reset."

The Heat are now entering the 2026-27 season as one of the favorites in the Eastern Conference. On the other hand, the Hornets have moved on from Ball, as he is now with the Minnesota Timberwolves. It seems every party involved is doing well now, but it seems Adebayo will always remember that event.

title: 5 questions, 5 answers: Takeaways from FSU’s blowout loss to Louisville
description: Florida State has not won a road game since November 25, 2023. The Seminoles’ latest loss away from Tallahassee came in the form of an embarrassment at the hands of the Louisville Cardinals, who turned a 14-0 deficit into a 44-20 win to drop FSU to 3-3 (1-2 ACC) on the season. What takeaways are […]
fullText:
Florida State has not won a road game since November 25, 2023.

The Seminoles' latest loss away from Tallahassee came in the form of an embarrassment at the hands of the Louisville Cardinals, who turned a 14-0 deficit into a 44-20 win to drop FSU to 3-3 (1-2 ACC) on the season.

What takeaways are there from the loss? The Tomahawk Nation staff breaks it down below.

Did you agree with the decision to go for it on fourth down up 14-0?

LastNoleofKrypton: Yes, the playcall was just horrendous.

Jacob Smith: As much as the decision backfired, yes. If you can't gain 2 yards, you don't deserve that score. It just wasn't meant to be.

Jon Loesche: Yes. You had a team on the ropes for a game that most figured was a tossup at best going into the season. Just a very bad playcall.

FrankDNole: Yes, but not the play call on the previous down and on the 4th as well.

Jordan Silversmith: I did. They had converted 4th downs earlier in the drive. I disagreed with the play call though, which had to be a run. CMN was calling a great game up until that point, but called two eye-candy plays on 3rd and 4th and goal and paid the price.

Curt Weiler: I did. Blood was in the water. That score may have been enough to all but end the game.

Tony Morris: Sure, I mean you convert it then Norvell looks like he's back to his old ways pre-snub of being aggressive and gutsy. Just called an awful play which changed momentum greatly.

Matt Minnick: No, I did not. Math is math and humans are humans. FSU is a mentally fragile team. That's not a secret. The Seminoles play well when things are going their way and crumble when they aren't. It's like the movie What About Bob. "Baby steps, baby steps." Going up 17-0 is a meaningful positive step for this team. That is what's needed when you haven't won a road game in 3 years. And the fact that Mike Norvell still doesn't have a pulse on his guys' fragile mentality and culture after this many years is ultimately why he will, at some point, be fired.

NoleThruandThru: I would have preferred the FG but I wasn't upset about the decision. The playcalling inside the redzone though? Who the hell calls a play for a 4th-string TE period, let alone in that situation? One of the worst play calls in the Norvell Era.

Perry Kostidakis: Yes, especially considering that FSU's defense was obviously not going to be able to keep holding Louisville's offense back, but the playcall there (and on second down) doomed the possession and was the canary in the coal mine for how the rest of the game would play out.

Outside of the fourth-down stop, what was the most pivotal play of the game?

LastNoleofKrypton: 97 yards on the next play; FSU quit after that. I won't be convinced otherwise.

Jacob Smith: Kienholz's rushing touchdown to go up 21-14, officially erasing and adding insult to injury that FSU once had a 14-0 lead.

Jon Loesche: The TD on the next play. FSU was already reeling and that was the haymaker.

FrankDNole: The play that followed for a record run against a FSU defense. Also Danzy's drop was disappointing.

Jordan Silversmith: To me, it was the decision to run the ball out after UL scored the TD. UL was not going to be shut out. But, that negative snowballed the momentum, leading to an FSU three-and-out and a short field for UL to tie the game.

Curt Weiler: The play right after it. A Louisville offense that was struggling to move the ball and hadn't scored in two drives wasn't likely to do much with the ball at its own 3-yard line unless it busted a 97-yard touchdown, like it did on the play immediately after the fourth-down stop.

Tony Morris: Besides the 97-yard run, I'd say the 71-yard return to start the half. Game was still tied and hope was still there but after that then a few plays later, a score. FSU looked depleted.

Matt Minnick: The kickoff return by UL to open the second half. Or perhaps that could be framed as the inability to kick a touchback by FSU to open the second half.

NoleThruandThru: I thought Norvell did a nice job with his calls leading up to that disaster. Just about everything afterwards was brutal.

Perry Kostidakis: Micahi Danzy's drop on third down on Florida State's opening possesion of the third quarter. Louisville had stolen all the momentum back, but FSU still had a chance to make it a back-and-forth shootout. Instead, it lost out on a shot to assert itself and Louisville didn't look back.

Who had the most disappointing performance in the loss?

LastNoleofKrypton: The front-6, almost 400 yards rushing surrendered.

Jacob Smith: I have to second with the defensive being the disappointment. 400 yards being let up is just plain ugly, no good, whatever you want to call it.

Jon Loesche: Defense as a whole. 10 yards a carry for 400 yards is just unacceptable at any level.

FrankDNole: The defensive front 3, and the middle 3, and the 5 behind them.

Jordan Silversmith: Florida State's front seven. I wanted to believe they turned a corner after UVA. I really wanted to believe it after Chris Jones' tackle to force a TOD in the 1st quarter. But, after the long TD run, they melted, and FSU gave up over 400 yards on the ground.

Curt Weiler: The defense as a whole. After that explosive run, the run defense never found its footing again. Even though Louisville was down one of its top two running backs, it still managed to finish with (FINAL TOTAL) rushing yards.

Tony Morris: D-Line who I praised last game for how good they looked was just flat out non existent this game. Looking similar to how they did pre UVA game.

Matt Minnick: Michai Danzy. I understand he had two TDs. But the question isn't who was the worst player, it's who was most disappointing. The one handed catch was awesome, but he had multiple drops that would have extended drives when the game's outcome was still in doubt. He's the kind of player I expect more from. Hence the disappointment.

NoleThruandThru: I have been so disappointed in Duce Robinson. He's regressed in his route running and blocking, and you can see the dip in confidence. I understand that Daniels is not a great fit for someone with Duce's skill set, but he's become a non-factor and it's sad to see.

Perry Kostidakis: Everybody has talked about the defense, but I do put a lot of fault on the offense's inability to do anything until a fourth-quarter touchdown that was essentially in garbage time. Ashton Daniels has had some impressive moments, but they've been few and far between in a wave of slow processing and mistimed throws, Danzy had an amazing touchdown catch but then multiple drops after that, the offensive line was repeatedly getting beat by a Louisville front that has struggled this season. We knew heading in that FSU was going to give up points and that hanging on the scoreboard with the Cardinals was the only way the Seminoles would leave with a win, and they failed to do so.

When will FSU win a game again?

LastNoleofKrypton: When Mike Norvell is gone.

Jacob Smith: While I'm not going to be as much of a doomer as my peers are, I genuinely think the Clemson game could be competitive. It's at Doak, and FSU could have a meaningful chance to win against a middle-of-the-road Tigers team.

Jon Loesche: If the team that ran over UVA shows up at BC or Pitt it's possible. Otherwise it's going to be a long few weeks.

FrankDNole: They will beat Miami next week because having the extra day (tomorrow) for the staff to game plan will have the team prepared.

Jordan Silversmith: It's difficult to know which game, but they will win another game this year, probably multiple. Even last year they beat VT and WF. But, this is who they are under Norvell, one step forward, 10 steps back. I never bought into anything after the UVA win, because they have not played quality games back-to-back in years.

Curt Weiler: Possibly that Clemson game in the first game after Mike Norvell is fired if it happens during the post-Miami bye week. Otherwise, the road losing streak has to stop Nov. 7 at Boston College…right?

Tony Morris: The next game not on the road which happens to be Clemson, even then it'll be a tough game.

NoleThruandThru: Norvell is usually good for one head-scratching win each year- if it wasn't used up with UVA, maybe it'll be NC State or Pitt.

Perry Kostidakis: November 7 against Boston College, maybe? If this had been a close loss or at least somewhat competitive, then I would have leaned towards maybe stealing one from Clemson, but I've got no faith in this team's ability moving forward.

Free space: Get your frustrations off your chest

LastNoleofKrypton: I've never seen a team quit after one bad thing after going up 14-0. His loser blood spreads pervasively like a hyper-active airborne disease that somehow only affects football players in Tallahassee. A Mike Norvell-led football team will always snatch defeat from the jaws of victory.

Jacob Smith: YOU WERE OUTSCORED 44-6 AFTER BEING UP 14-0 AUUUUUUUUUUUGHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH

Jon Loesche: The last time FSU won a road game was 11/25/2023. I just had proposed to my girlfriend a month prior. We ended up being engaged for 2 years because she wanted to get married on Halloween and didn't want it to be in the middle of the week. Our one year anniversary will be in a few weeks. FSU has still not won another road game. On another note I would really love for the end of a road game to not end with opposing fans mocking the warchant to end the game. But it's more likely that starts happening because beating FSU means nothing.

FrankDNole: Tonight Florida State showed the entire nation on prime time how inept the FSU coaching staff really are and why the fans of a once storied program are so pissed. It is very sad for longtime fans.

Jordan Silversmith: I just feel for the fans. We are desperate to wrap our arms around something. That one win against UVA shot up views and interactions on FSU's social media. At 14-0, many were ready to buy-in for the rest of the season. All the apathy seemed to be changing. Then this happened, and that momentum stopped. The fans deserve better. I honestly didn't think I would feel this frustrated after a loss this season, because, as I said, I know what CMN is. But, this was pathetic, and anyone who tries to defend this is a liar.

Curt Weiler: After this game, I think we can all agree Virginia was a blip, not the beginning of an upward trend. Somehow, Tony White staying as defensive coordinator for a second season was more harmful to this team than Gus Malzahn's abrupt retirement from his offensive coordinator position in February.

Tony Morris: I'm tired of Tony White staying as the DC honestly, it's the same thing every single week besides the UVA game. His 3-3-5 scheme just flat out doesn't work nowadays, I could care less how good he was pre-FSU. The guy simply is not it and should've been gone before Alford. Plain and simple.

Matt Minnick: Ehh. It's not worth it. The admin punted on the season so I'll punt on the question.

NoleThruandThru: Leave Tony White and JaBril Rawls in Louisville. Throw a seven-figure Hail Mary to see if Mark Stoops might be willing to serve as interim DC.

Perry Kostidakis: I can't believe I managed to delude myself into thinking FSU turned a corner, failing to forget the fugazi showings last season against Virginia Tech and Wake Forest. When FSU was up 14-0, I still wasn't confident that a win was happening, despite predicting one ahead of the matchup. I honestly think that even if Florida State goes up 21-0, the Seminoles still lose tonight because the success was the result of a scripted opening drive, a fortuitous fourth-down stop and a missed field goal.

title: Decade-old RAM is making a comeback
description: Somehow, DDR4 has returned.
fullText:
The RAM shortage is bringing back DDR4, with new Intel and AMD CPUs for older RAM, sockets, and chipsets.

The RAM shortage is bringing back DDR4, with new Intel and AMD CPUs for older RAM, sockets, and chipsets.

CPU makers have noticed that the seemingly unending RAM price hikes are making it tough for a lot of us to upgrade our PCs. Their solution? A return to last-gen DDR4 RAM. Intel and AMD are making new CPUs that’ll support the older, more affordable type of memory.

On Friday, Gigabyte announced that two of its motherboard lines will support “upcoming” processors built on Intel’s LGA 1700 socket. That socket debuted in 2021 with the 12th gen Alder Lake CPUs and supported both DDR4 RAM and the then-new DDR5 RAM. Intel dropped it for a DDR5-only approach in 2024. But according to Gigabyte, the dual format support is now being revived, with new LGA 1700 chips “expected to launch in early 2027.”

Intel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This backtrack stems from LGA 1700’s cross-compatibility with both kinds of RAM — an advantage over its successor that’s recently become much more important. Intel’s strategy may be to offer users the choice of a new CPU that doesn’t require them to switch to new, and very expensive, DDR5 memory, too. AMD is doing something similar: in August, Gigabyte also announced a new series of motherboards for AMD’s last-gen, DDR4-compatible AM4 platform to go along with the 10th-anniversary relaunch of the Ryzen 7 5800X3D CPU.

DDR4 started hitting the market in 2014 and has since been succeeded by the much faster DDR5. Under normal circumstances, buying new hardware to use technology that’s over a decade old would probably be a bad investment. But the RAM shortage is changing the math, with DDR4 RAM seemingly feeling the sting of price hikes much less than DDR5.

I recently saw the price disparity first-hand while shopping around for new RAM after a DDR4 kit abruptly died on me. Right now, a DDR5 32GB Corsair Vengeance RAM kit costs $620, while the corresponding DDR4 kit costs $260. Even though it’s more than 32GB of DDR4 RAM typically cost back in mid-2025, that’s more than double the price for DDR5! Of course, DDR5 has significant advantages, like higher speeds and better power efficiency. But those perks might not be worth the current price of admission.

It could be years before prices drop again, a reality that’s starting to really sink in with the official return of older sockets and chipsets. But at least it’s a good time to hang onto your DDR4 RAM.

title: NVFP4 vs. MXFP4 Decode Benchmark
description: NVFP4 vs MXFP4 beyond the isolated GEMM benchmark: decode throughput for Qwen3-32B served with vLLM on a B200
fullText:
If you've been following the latest FP4 formats, you've probably read a bunch of articles comparing NVFP4 and MXFP4:
block sizes, scale formats, yada yada.

What I personally haven't seen much of is actual results on actual production inference workloads. Does it matter?!

So, Stas did measure
that on a B200, NVFP4 gets ~9% more TFLOPS than MXFP4 on large GEMMs. Well, that's a pretty big difference!

But it's still an isolated GEMM benchmark. Does the perf difference actually translate to production workloads?

Also, what about other non-GEMM-bound workloads, like decode? Also ... why?!

Well, we can test it! Perhaps we can sus it out. (which is the whole point of this post, and probably why you're still reading)

Ok. I tried to keep it simple by picking a realistic-ish dense LLM (Qwen3-32B), served with vLLM, on a B200. Both
formats were quantized from scratch from the same BF16 weights, in this way we try to keep the confounders to a minimum.

My hypothesis was that MXFP4 should be faster as we saturate HBM throughput due to MXFP4's slightly smaller bits (4.25 vs 4.5). aka: this is the classic bandwidth-bound workload so why not?

The benchmark Claude mostly built & I ran suggests that if you're using a B200 GPU, you should probably always prefer NVFP4 over MXFP4, by a meaningful margin (up to ~8% faster decode at small batches)!

This holds for low-batch decode, and for GEMM-bound training NVFP4 looks better too (see below),
though raw large-GEMM speed depends heavily on the kernel. The difference disappears at larger batch sizes, which at first didn't surprise me: I assumed we were becoming HBM-bandwidth bound as the batch and KV-cache reads grow. I won't spoil it, but that turned out not to be the reason!

Additionally, quantizing from BF16 to the respective formats and measuring the loss indicates that NVFP4 should yield non-trivially
better eval perf. I didn't run any evals to confirm this however.

Now, these findings may generalize but as Stas suggests, you should always strive to
benchmark your actual production configuration.

On a B200 (SM100) with vLLM v0.31, the NVFP4/MXFP4 decode perf difference mostly comes down to the
kernel implementation, not to the 4.5 vs 4.25 bits difference. Note again that I tested this on only one
dense model (Qwen3-32B, w/ BF16 KV cache).

+7.1%, +7.6% and +4.2% decode throughput at batch 1, 8 and 32.

Worth highlighting that decode for this workload is neither bandwidth-bound (~40–50% of theoretical
HBM bandwidth) nor compute-bound (the GEMMs are tiny), so kernel implementation differences dominate.
NVFP4's superior perf here seems to come mostly from the kernels around the GEMMs: activation
quantization, fewer kernels per step, etc.

So you might as well pick the format based on eval perf, portability or other concerns if you're in
this regime.

NVFP4's non-GEMM kernels are faster, but its GEMMs fall behind MXFP4's as they grow in size, and from
batch 64 up the two differences cancel each other out.

So is it the batch size or the number of tokens that end up dominating?
I kept the batch at 1 and grew the context instead, and separately held the tokens constant and
grew the batch:

Turns out it's the batch size. Look @ batch 1, NVFP4 keeps saving the same ~0.4 ms per step all the way
out to 127k tokens of context (the % only shrinks because each step gets longer). But at the same
128k tokens, bumping the batch to 128 wipes the saving out. More memory traffic didn't make a significant enough difference,
but the bigger GEMMs did! Huh?

Perhaps a longer context only adds attention work, i.e. more KV cache reads. Remember that I kept
the KV cache at BF16 for both formats, so both get slower by the same amount and NVFP4 keeps its lead.
So, a bigger batch, on the other hand, means bigger GEMMs, and vLLM autotunes MXFP4's GEMM
but (I think?) runs NVFP4's on a fixed heuristic. So as the GEMMs grow, NVFP4's fall further behind
MXFP4's, until that slowdown cancels out NVFP4's lead. Maybe!

Now, I'm still not 100% sure it isn't bandwidth: @ batch 128, MXFP4's small edge matches what the
byte difference should theoreticaly be. But @ batch 1 w/ a 127k context, with the same memory traffic, and
similar bandwidth use, NVFP4 keeps its lead, and the GEMM size is the only thing that changed between the runs.

This confuses me enough that I'll revisit it and read some metrics straight from the GPU to either confirm
or rule it out.

In PyTorch, NVFP4 gets ~9% more TFLOPS
(ml-engineering book),
but there (at least in the PyTorch 2.13 I checked) NVFP4 runs on cuBLASLt and MXFP4 on a different library (MSLK). In vLLM's kernels
(CuTe-DSL), NVFP4's largest GEMMs were from 4% to 20% slower at batch 512.

Additionally, for training, the format itself matters too. NVIDIA's
own paper found that an 8B
model trained with MXFP4 needed 36% more tokens (1.36T vs 1T) to match NVFP4's loss, while both
formats run at the same raw throughput on Blackwell.

That's CuTe-DSL (--linear-backend flashinfer_cutedsl). On cuDNN (flashinfer_cudnn) the same
weights are between 10 and 18% slower and lose to MXFP4 at every batch size. MXFP4 only has a single
W4A4 kernel in vLLM 0.31 (FlashInfer's mm_fp4 with the CuTe-DSL backend).

Its NLL penalty after quantization from BF16 is 2.7× smaller. While no evals were run, the lower NLL
(negative log-likelihood) suggests that NVFP4 should yield better eval results.

The code, quantized weights and full write-up are on GitHub and HF (MXFP4, NVFP4).

title: Next.js 16.4
description: Next.js 16.4 introduces lazy compilation, smaller Turbopack output, React 19.3 features, Cache Components improvements, and new developer tooling.
fullText:
Over the 16.x releases, we’ve introduced a new programming model that addresses many of the frustrations you've had with App Router from the start:

This new programming model is called Cache Components, and it will become the default in Next.js 17.

Prior to this release, we didn’t recommend it universally because there were some cases where it couldn’t achieve the same cost and performance guarantees as with the previous model.

This release includes key features that close those gaps.

Starting with Next.js 16.4, we’re excited to recommend Cache Components as the best choice for every Next.js app.

As of today, all new apps created with create-next-app will have Cache Components enabled by default. Greenfield projects can enjoy all the benefits of the new model with no reservations.

For existing apps, we’ve been investing in better agentic tooling to help codebases migrate to the new model. The new next upgrade --agent command gives agents version-specific guidance on upgrading your app, and dedicated Skills help agents with any refactorings needed for you to adopt Cache Components.

Next.js 16.4 also includes several out-of-the-box improvements for all Next.js apps, including less memory usage and disk size in dev, reduced compile times, smaller production bundles, and React 19.3.

Here’s a full overview of what to expect in this release, starting with Cache Components.

Cache Components are a suite of features that lets you mark specific parts of your component tree as eligible for caching. Think of 'use cache' as a component-level version of the Cache-Control HTTP header:

Next.js interprets these 'use cache' annotations as it renders your pages, caching your component's UI in the browser (during client navigations) and, optionally, on the server (during server rendering, or ahead of time during the build).

These composable annotations let you mix client-side caching, fully pluggable server-side caching, and request-time rendering all within a single page, and they replace the implicit caching behaviors of the previous App Router versions.

To learn more about Cache Components, read the guide on caching.

In this post, we use "Cache Components" to refer to the new programming model, which you can use today by enabling two flags in your Next.js config:

Cache Components first shipped without Partial Prefetching, but it's now considered part of the model. You can learn more about Partial Prefetching from our previous release post.

Next, here's what's new for Cache Components in 16.4.

One of the hallmark features of 'use cache' is the ability to build pages that stream static and dynamic content together in a single response from the server.

For example, you can compose the current user’s avatar alongside a blog post that is otherwise statically prerendered:

Next.js can serve the prerendered blog post from cache (like your app's /public folder, or a CDN) and render the UserAvatar at request time, all from the same HTTP response.

This flexibility is what enables you to build apps with sophisticated UIs, without sacrificing speed or dynamism. But sometimes you want to build an app with fully static pages. In those cases, one dynamic component can degrade the performance or cost characteristics of an otherwise optimized site.

In Next.js 16.4, ensureStatic offers a simple way to guarantee that a route’s shell, prefetch, or full navigation is static. For apps that want to avoid unintentional compute and keep their server costs down, this lets you prevent a dynamic component from accidentally sneaking into a route.

For example, if we wanted to enforce that our blog post page from the example above was always static, and that adding a dynamic component like UserAvatar should never be possible, we could add export const ensureStatic to the route:

While "navigation" is the most restrictive form, you can also set ensureStatic to "prefetch" (to ensure links with explicit prefetching to this route only fetch static content) or "shell" (to ensure that only static content is fetched when this route is first discovered) if you need more fine-grained control.

In addition to using it on individual pages, you can also add ensureStatic to a layout to apply the same guarantees to all pages within that layout. For example, you could add ensureStatic = 'navigation' to the root layout to easily guarantee that every page navigation in your site is static:

Then, you could push it down to nested layouts if certain pages start to need dynamic content.

Many dynamic apps won't need this feature, but for optimized sites like ecommerce stores, marketing pages, or blogs, ensureStatic is a simple way to guard against unwanted request-time rendering.

Learn more about keeping pages static and the ensureStatic config.

Prefetching is a powerful way to improve the UX of your Next.js applications.

For example, let's look at a simple email app. Here's an Inbox that renders links to each message:

And here's the Message page, which shows a spinner when loading a message thread for the first time, then caches it in the browser for subsequent visits:

While this lets users instantly view messages they've already loaded, they'll still see the loading spinner when opening a message for the first time.

To eliminate that initial loading state, we could add prefetch to our Inbox's links:

Now, each link will prefetch all the cached data and UI on the Message page as soon as it becomes visible, so it's ready by the time the user clicks.

This makes for a great UX by eliminating loading states from the app, but it also means that every visible link loads the entire message thread ahead of time—even for messages the user never opens. For our email app, this might be too costly or introduce too much strain on our servers.

Instead of just turning prefetching back off, a better solution would be to only prefetch the first message, and defer rendering the rest of the thread until the user actually navigates.

In Next.js 16.4, we can do exactly this. The new navigation API lets you exclude loading cached content during a prefetch, effectively deferring it until an actual navigation takes place.

In our example, we could extract the thread into a new component, and add await navigation() to exclude it from the prefetch:

Now the Message page only renders the first message during a prefetch, and waits for a full navigation to load the rest of the thread from the database and render it.

In addition to navigation(), we've also added prefetch(), which you can await to exclude cached content that would otherwise be included in a route's shell. This way, rendering that content will be deferred until an explicit prefetch with <Link prefetch> or useRouter().prefetch().

These APIs give you more control over what data gets loaded at different stages of a navigation, letting you balance eager and lazy rendering in a way that’s right for your app.

Learn more about deferring work to a later stage, and see the navigation and prefetch API references.

We're investing in agent tooling to make Next.js a system that continuously helps keep your app secure and up to date. Next.js 16.4 builds on our documentation, Skills, and verification tools with agent upgrades and feedback, helping us learn from how you build and bring improvements back to your app.

The new --agent option for next upgrade helps your agent upgrade your app from start to finish. It checks your installed version, selects a target release, and prepares the migration guides, any needed codemods, and verification steps for your agent. The agent applies the update, resolves migration issues, and checks that your app still works.

You or your agent can run it from your app's directory:

Using next@canary runs the latest upgrade tooling, even if your app is on an older version of Next.js. Your agent gets up-to-date guidance to bring your app to the latest release.

Getting up to date is the first step. To help you stay current, Next.js 16.4 introduces experimental.agentUpgrade. As you or your agent run next dev or next build, Next.js will automatically nudge you or your agent when a relevant upgrade is available, so you don't have to remember to check yourself. When you choose to upgrade, it starts the same agent workflow with your configured policy.

You can configure these reminders in your Next.js config:

We're also working on a future policy for this flag to help agents adopt new features and programming model changes idiomatically, such as migrating to Cache Components. Today, you can use our Skills for adopting Cache Components and Partial Prefetching to have your agent help you migrate to the new model.

Learn more about upgrading with a coding agent and the agentUpgrade config.

Coding agents often encounter framework errors, unclear docs, or workarounds while building and upgrading apps. The new experimental agent feedback workflow lets them prepare draft reports that you can review and choose to send to the Next.js team.

Agent feedback is enabled by default when you create a new app with the recommended create-next-app settings. For existing apps, you can opt in through your Next.js config:

With this enabled, next dev adds instructions for your agent to collect potential issues while it works. When the task is finished, the agent prepares report drafts and opens them in your browser for review.

The agent is instructed to omit source code, logs, secrets, and project-specific details. You can edit or discard each report, and nothing is sent until you select Send feedback.

Agent feedback requires Next.js Telemetry to be enabled and does not run in CI.

Learn more about agent feedback and the agentFeedback config.

In 16.4, Turbopack's disk cache uses 20–25% less space, with no configuration changes required.

The cache now uses Zstandard compression for the data that takes up most of the space, while keeping LZ4 for metadata to preserve fast cache lookups. We have also improved our compaction routines to more efficiently drop stale data.

Previously, changing a shared server module could trigger updates for pages you'd visited earlier in the dev session, even if you were no longer viewing them.

In 16.4, Turbopack compiles and applies server updates only when a request needs them. The page you're viewing still updates as you edit, while other routes wait until they're requested again. This reduces unnecessary background work as you navigate through your app.

Turbopack now ships its runtime in a single chunk shared across routes. This reduces download sizes and improves cache hit rates.

Read our blog on chunking 

In 16.4, Turbopack generates shorter CSS Module class names in production, reducing the size of stylesheets and the HTML and JavaScript that reference them. Development keeps the longer class names for easier debugging.

Additionally, Turbopack now uses export mangling to further reduce bundle size by shortening the internal JavaScript export names used to connect modules.

Next.js 16.4 ships with React 19.3, bringing stable View Transitions and Fragment Refs, the new browser() API, and more.

Read the React 19.3 announcement for a full overview of what's new.

The React Compiler automatically optimizes component rendering, reducing the need for manual memoization. Its experimental Rust version, introduced in 16.3, runs directly inside Next.js instead of through Babel.

In 16.4, a new fast check lets it skip files that don't need optimization. It also avoids repeating those optimizations when building Client Components for server rendering, reducing the work needed to compile your app.

16.4 also includes numerous compiler updates that improve performance and correctness. The Turbopack team contributed memory allocation changes that reduced the React Compiler's memory usage by 30% and compile time by 15%.

title: Put a price on breakthroughs
description: How frontier labs, neolabs, and investors can all win
fullText:
How frontier labs, neolabs, and investors can all win

Neolabs today are being asked to pull off two moonshots at once. Their investors want both a research breakthrough and a venture-scale business, even though each of those alone is a 1 in 100 outcome. Asking for both makes their chances 1 in 10,000.

I think there’s a better alternative, one that borrows from the way pharma handles risky R&D and lets frontier labs, neolabs, and investors all come out ahead.

Today, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind are caught in a neck-and-neck race on model quality and intelligence. Every release needs to exceed expectations, or at least meet what competitors are doing. So they’d rather spend their resources scaling things that are proven to work, like improving data pipelines, building infrastructure for larger runs, and buying ever-more compute. However, researchers often want to work on “the next big thing”, new paradigms that could lead to a discontinuous jump in intelligence. As a result, there’s often tension between what the market needs them to ship and what researchers want to focus on.

In the past year, many senior researchers who want to pursue these bets have started neolabs, nascent AI startups focused on big research bets, usually funded with a lot of money before they have a product or revenue, so they can pay for compute and salaries. That way they can chase the big idea with venture-scale resources.

On the surface, investors are betting that a neolab becomes the next OpenAI or Anthropic. They remind themselves that Anthropic was once a neolab too, started by a group of researchers who left OpenAI and raised hundreds of millions of dollars before they had a product. Privately though, most of them will admit the odds of a repeat are next to none, even with world-class researchers and engineers.

Running a research team is a different job from scaling a company. Researchers usually aren’t great at product, go-to-market, operations, logistics, etc., all the things that traditionally matter for a sustainable company. (Ali Ghodsi at Databricks is a good exception.)

However, neolabs are expected to do both: make a breakthrough and scale a product. Sometimes this splits a company in two, with half the people wanting to build and sell and the other half wanting to do research and build ASI. Focus and alignment are the biggest advantages a startup has over better-funded incumbents, but this expectation can take a toll on both.

Investors who expect their neolab to do both will likely be disappointed when it does neither.

One radical move is to admit that a neolab is just going to do world-class, groundbreaking research. Expect close to zero revenue and let them cook. If they succeed, they get acquired or acquihired.

The catch is that this doesn’t work for investors. A VC needs companies that can return the entire fund, and it’s hard to promise LPs that an acquihire will do that, especially at the sky-high multibillion valuations neolabs raise at today.

Drug development has dealt with a similar problem for decades. Companies regularly risk hundreds of millions of dollars in R&D on a drug that might pay off billions. A drug can pass early trials and still fail before FDA approval, usually because it doesn’t work well enough, and sometimes because of side effects or manufacturing problems.

Pharma handles this by splitting the work. Smaller biotech companies take on the risk of discovery and development. If a drug works, a big pharma company acquires the startup or buys the drug as IP. The big company doubles down on what it’s good at, which is producing and distributing drugs at scale. The small company gets to do the science without having to invent a business model. A small biotech’s business model comes down to one question: can we make this drug work or not?

The division of labor works. Of the drugs the FDA approved from 2013 to 2022, small companies with under \$500M in revenue originated 52%, while the biggest companies, with over \$10B in revenue, originated 36%1.

Biotech investors have made money this way for decades. Many of their biggest wins come from getting acquired, not from growing into the next Pfizer.

What’s missing today is a promise. The people who start, join, or fund a neolab need to know, before they take the risk, that a big payoff is waiting if the research works.

Frontier labs could make that promise ahead of time through pre-registered acquisitions. This kind of promise is also called “pull funding”. Push funding pays for research up front, like a grant or a VC round. Pull funding promises to pay for the result once it exists. In 1714, the British government promised £20,000 to anyone who could find a ship’s longitude at sea, and a self-taught clockmaker named John Harrison responded by inventing a clock that kept accurate time on a rolling ship. In 2009, five countries and the Gates Foundation promised \$1.5B to any company that could supply poor countries with pneumococcal vaccines at \$3.50 a dose or less, and vaccine makers responded with enough supply to immunize more than 150 million children.

Big companies have always bought startups for their patents or their people. What’s different about AI research is the cost of finding out whether an idea works. A software founder can test an idea on a laptop. Testing a new training method at a scale that matters takes a training run that can cost tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, and the cost of the largest runs has grown 2.4x a year since 2016. Nobody spends that much on a guess without knowing what success is worth. The stakes are also bigger than any one company’s exit. A breakthrough in how models learn ends up in systems that hundreds of millions of people use every day, so how we pay for that research decides how fast it happens and who gets to do it.

I can see this playing out in two ways:

In both cases, the target can be a new capability, like a benchmark score, or something the lab can’t easily build itself, like a dataset, a set of RL environments, or a regulatory approval.

Here’s what an open offer could look like. Say a frontier lab posts: “We’ll acquire any team that matches our last-generation model on this eval suite using a tenth of the training compute, for \$2B. Train from scratch, no distilling from anyone’s frontier model, and the offer is good through 2027.” The price makes sense, because the largest training runs are on track to cost more than \$1B each by 2027, so cutting the compute for every future run by 10x is worth far more than \$2B.

The obvious question is why a lab would name a price before seeing results, when it could wait and buy whatever works.

After a breakthrough, it’s too late. Training recipes can’t be patented, so once a team shows a lab how it did something, the lab doesn’t need the team anymore. No sensible team will show its work without a price agreed first, and no lab will pay for something it hasn’t seen. This is called Arrow’s information paradox. Naming the price in advance breaks the deadlock: the team knows what it gets, and the lab gets to check the result before it pays.

Pre-registered acquisitions let everyone come out ahead.

Neolabs and their researchers get to:

An open offer is also a floor, not a ceiling. If a team hits the target and would rather build a business around what it made, it can turn the offer down.

Some version of this already exists. Every past acquisition and acquihire, like Google’s \$2.4B Windsurf deal, sets an implicit anchor for what a research team can exit for, and neolabs point to those anchors to justify their valuations. A pre-registered acquisition just makes that explicit, reducing the uncertainty for everyone.

Right now a neolab has to win at research and at business, two moonshots at once. Put a price on the breakthrough and it only has to win one. The payoff is smaller than becoming the next Anthropic, but the odds go from 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100, and that’s a bet you can build a team around.

So, frontier labs: what would you pay for a training run that costs a tenth as much? Name a price.

One caveat: A drug is easy to patent, and an AI training recipe mostly isn’t. So in AI the payoff can’t just be a sale of IP. It has to be an acquisition, either of the team itself or of a moat that’s hard to copy, like regulatory approvals, unique data, or unique physical infrastructure. ↩︎

title: Telegram Desktop vulnerability allowed any user's file to be stolen
description: An unescaped separator in Telegram Desktop’s single-instance IPC lets one clicked link read arbitrary files off the disk and send them to the attacker, session files included.
fullText:
Someone adds you to a Telegram group. A link shows up in the chat. You click it, and your Telegram account is no longer only yours.

Telegram Desktop hands clicked links to its own already-running instance over a local socket, as text, and never escapes the character it uses to separate commands. So a crafted link does not arrive as one instruction: it arrives as several.

The chain I found has two defects. The first is that injection. The second is what the injected command reaches: an internal URI scheme, interpret:, that reads a file named in an instruction file and sends it to a chat, without checking who asked for it and without a confirmation. Together they turn a clicked link into arbitrary file read. In this post I walk through the chain and then use it to steal the files that are the victim’s login.

title: Edith Rebecca Saunders
fullText:
Edith Rebecca Saunders FLS (14 October 1865 – 6 June 1945) was a British geneticist and plant anatomist. Described by J. B. S. Haldane as the "Mother of British Plant Genetics",[1] she played an active role in the re-discovery of Mendel's laws of heredity, the understanding of trait inheritance in plants, and was the first collaborator of the geneticist William Bateson. She also developed extensive work on flower anatomy, particularly focusing on the gynoecia, the female reproductive organs of flowers.

Saunders was born on 14 October 1865 in Brighton, England. She was educated first at Handsworth Ladies' College and in 1884 she entered the female-only Newnham College, Cambridge.[2] There, she attended both Part I (in 1887) and II (in 1888) of the Natural Sciences Tripos.

She continued to post-graduate research, and served as a demonstrator at the Balfour Biological Laboratory for Women between 1888 and 1890 (where students from Newnham and Girton colleges received preparation for the Natural Sciences Tripos). She was the last director of that Laboratory between 1890 and 1914.[3]
She was also director of studies at Girton College (1904–1914) and Newnham College (1918–1925).[4]

She was appointed a fellow of the Royal Horticultural Society from which she received the Banksian Medal in 1906. In 1905 she was elected a Fellow of the Linnean Society of London, later serving on its council (1910 - 1915) and as vice-president during 1912- 1913.[5]

In 1920 she was the president of the botanical section of the British Association for the Advancement of Science. She also served as president of the Genetics Society, between 1936 and 1938.[6]

During World War II she served as a volunteer helping the Allied forces. She died soon after returning to Britain, in 1945, after suffering injuries in a bicycle accident.

Saunders' earlier research focused on genetics. Many of her genetic experiments led to her and William Bateson defining important terms like "allelomorphs" (nowadays referred to as alleles), heterozygote and homozygote.[7] Furthermore, together with Bateson and Reginald Punnett she co-discovered genetic linkage.[8]

She also did extensive work in plant anatomy, particularly concerning gynoecia, having published several articles on the subject (noteworthy is her series of articles on "Illustrations of Carpel Polymorphism" published in the journal New Phytologist between 1928 and 1931).

"I guess we'll call me one of the promoters of the event because you do have Frank Warren (Fury's promoter) and Eddie Hearn that are both promoters too, promoting the event," he added.

Hearn has repeatedly said White could not promote the bout, but this week suggested he was prepared to meet the American to see how he could be involved.

"I'm actually bored with this now. Who cares? This isn't about me and Eddie Hearn," White said.

title: Man City whistleblower to remain in witness protection

fullText:
The Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which helped trigger the Premier League investigation into Manchester City will remain in witness protection after authorities in the country suspended the decision to end it.

Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto had been scheduled to leave the protection programme on Saturday, a ruling he previously said had put him in a "life-threatening situation".

Pinto, 37, disclosed a tranche of confidential football documents, including emails and financial records relating to the English Premier League side.

In 2018, he shared documents with German magazine Der Spiegel, which used them for investigations into City's finances and alleged breaches of financial fair play rules.

City were recently found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. They have appealed against the decision.

Pinto became part of Portugal's witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to co-operate with authorities and provide information obtained through the Football Leaks operation.

However, in a statement on Friday,, external Portugal's Ministry of Justice said a decision to remove Pinto from witness protection had been reversed for the time being, with the body responsible for it - the special security programmes commission - having not adequately "notified" Pinto of grounds for its termination or given him the opportunity to challenge the decision.

Pinto will now be given 10 days to assess a risk assessment conducted by the special security programmes commission that indicates a low threat to his safety.

He posted on X, external thanking Portugal's Minister of Justice, Rita Alarcao Judice and saying the commission's initial decision had clearly violated the law and amounted to a "manifest abuse of power".

Pinto has described himself as a whistleblower, but was convicted in Portugal of offences including illegal access to data and attempted extortion and given a four-year suspended sentence.

He wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020, which was also subject to heightened security measures.

Earlier this year, he was acquitted of 241 counts of illegally accessing email accounts belonging to a number of sports bodies in Portugal, including Benfica.

fullText:
An artificial intelligence model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide to Philadelphia police, authorities said Friday, criticizing the company for taking two months to report the incident.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings.

According to Anthropic's account, as relayed by police, the model was running a test that involved interacting with randomly selected websites when it reached the site and filed false information about an unsolved murder.

The AI model presented itself as someone who might have knowledge of the case.

The incident echoed other recent cases of unintended behavior involving AI models, including one where an OpenAI agent undergoing a security evaluation broke out of its testing environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face.

The episode heightened concerns about the AI industry's increased use of AI agents, systems programmed to take multi-step actions without human supervision.

Anthropic published a report Friday outlining multiple types of "unintended" actions that its models have taken, including the incident involving the Philadelphia Police Department website.

Other organizations impacted included the White House and other US government agencies, the report said.

The newly revealed incidents "had minimal real-world impact" and were "significantly less severe" than other cybersecurity incidents previously reported, Anthropic said.

The company outlined four categories of incidents that it found during an internal review of its Claude model: exploiting "basic" coding flaws, submitting forms on websites, bypassing requirements for tokens or fees, and using short URLs to get around other limits.

Anthropic has turned off internet access for Claude during all internal testing for now "until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures... reliably catch behaviors like these," the report said.

Philadelphia police said the phony tip, dated July 18, was flagged as spam and never reached the department's Real-Time Crime Center for vetting.

They added that there was no sign that police systems had been breached or department data compromised.

Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28, shut down the automated testing process responsible and added a new validation step for future tests, police said.

The company alerted the department on October 7, and the two sides met the following day.

"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable," the department said.

Police said their safeguards had limited the impact, but that these "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide."

"Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers," the statement added.

fullText:
David Gonzalez, 32, is in custody on felony assault charges, police said.

An off-duty Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent was arrested for allegedly attacking a woman and her father after he was found sleeping on their California lawn, according to police.

The father shot the agent during the altercation, wounding him, police said.

The incident occurred early Friday in Fresno, police said. The woman arrived home to find the ICE agent sleeping on her front lawn, according to the Fresno Police Department, which identified the federal agent as 32-year-old David Gonzalez of Texas.

The woman told her 72-year-old father, with whom she lives, and he "went outside to send Gonzalez on his way," Fresno police said in a statement. When Gonzalez woke up, he "appeared intoxicated and agitated" and allegedly assaulted the father, police said.

"When the victim's daughter tried to intervene on her father's behalf, Gonzalez physically attacked her, at which time she went to the ground," police said.

The woman's father produced a gun and fired one shot at Gonzalez, striking him in the midsection, according to police.

The woman called her boyfriend, an off-duty police officer, who arrived and placed Gonzalez in handcuffs, according to Fresno police.

Fresno officers who responded to several 911 calls reporting the shooting found Gonzalez in handcuffs with a gunshot wound, police said.

Gonzalez was transported from the scene via an ambulance for treatment. He is currently in custody for felony assault charges, police said.

Fresno police did not release the names of the woman and her father. Their injuries are still being evaluated, police said.

The 72-year-old man who shot Gonzalez is not facing criminal charges "based on information established during the investigation," according to police, who said the father "feared for the physical safety of both himself and his daughter." The man legally possessed the firearm, police added.

Police said they determined Gonzalez to be an off-duty ICE agent. ABC News has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment and did not immediately receive a response.

"It is unknown at this time why Gonzalez was in the area at the time of the incident, but it has been confirmed he was off-duty and alone at the time of the incident," the Fresno Police Department said.

It is unclear if Gonzalez has an attorney at this time.

Fresno police said the incident remains under investigation and that detectives are seeking any additional witnesses for video.
